analysis.title: Just the FAQs (Blog, Jason Draho)
key_insights: Last Thursday's roughly 4% S&P 500 selloff was driven more by positioning, retail and levered ETF selling and systematic deleveraging than by fundamentals. No major economic, policy or corporate news was released that day.

Credit spreads barely widened on the selloff day. UBS says investment grade spreads should have widened closer to 10bps on a 4% S&P 500 drop if fundamentals were deteriorating. The VIX rose 70%, far more than its six-month relationship to the S&P 500 implies, which suggests investors were buying downside protection that amplified the equity move.

Midterm election implications: Democrats in Congress will push to rescind One Big Beautiful Bill spending cuts due to start in 2027 as part of funding the government and raising the debt ceiling. Success could add about 20bps to GDP growth versus the low baseline forecast.
President Trump keeps considerable discretion on trade, regulation and foreign policy and could moderate or double down on existing policies.

The most significant midterm implication for markets is greater AI regulation. State and local governments can slow or halt data center buildout, and new Democratic Governors in Texas, Georgia and Michigan could introduce temporary restrictions. Those three states hold roughly 45% of planned US data center capacity, about 25% in Texas alone.

UBS argues data center regulation aims to make data centers more self-reliant on electricity generation, grid infrastructure and water, not to stop them. Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa said currently permitted Texas data centers can finish construction and acknowledged limited ability to impose a moratorium. The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality controls permits.

UBS expects new regulation to slow AI investment only marginally, with the effect more likely in 2028 and 2029 because most planned 2027 spending is already approved. A real AI investment slowdown is more likely to come from bottlenecks in energy, capital, semiconductors, or insufficient compute demand.

October nonfarm payrolls rose 165k, well above expectations, and August and September were revised higher. The 3-month average payroll growth rose to 137k from 51k. UBS sees Q4/Q4 growth around 2.5% in 2026, moderating toward 2% in 2027.
UBS expects the Fed to keep raising rates given solid growth and gradual disinflation, with another 25bps hike in December and again in March.

Medium-term outlook stays positive but near-term volatility is likely until there is policy clarity and confidence that AI investment and returns continue. Institutional investors appear reluctant to buy the selloff ahead of year-end. UBS expects S&P 500 earnings to grow nearly 15% next year and recommends using volatility to add diversified exposure to higher-quality companies.

Retail selling was unusually heavy that morning, as was selling in levered ETFs, and systematic strategies increased selling through the day.
Institutional investors appear reluctant to buy the selloff, partly from unwillingness to take risk before year-end.

tension_points.bull_case: Regulation aims to make data centers self-reliant, not stop them. Permitted Texas data centers can finish construction, the Texas governor-elect has limited power to impose a moratorium, and most 2027 spending is already approved, so the slowdown is marginal and mostly in 2028-2029.
tension_points.bear_case: State and local governments can slow or halt buildout. Texas, Georgia and Michigan hold about 45% of planned US data center capacity, and new Democratic governors could introduce temporary restrictions, which adds to existing concerns about AI investment pace and financing costs.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A real AI investment slowdown from bottlenecks in energy, capital, semiconductors, or insufficient compute demand, or temporary restrictions introduced by the new Democratic Governors in Texas, Georgia and Michigan.
